network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, atom-balanced candidate network, not a demonstrated complete prebiotic synthesis. The supplied evidence does not establish ten experimentally validated pathways to free glutamine. Accordingly, the ten pathways below are explicitly conditional graph routes: two literature-supported precursor-entry branches combined with five chemically distinguishable, but unvalidated, timings of nitrile hydration and Strecker chemistry. Their enumeration does not multiply the experimental evidence. The network uses surface environments because precursor photochemistry is supported there and hot hydrothermal residence would threaten glutamine preservation. Glutamine has five carbons; the report's ambiguous references to a C4 aminodinitrile are corrected here to 2-aminopentanedinitrile. All listed transformations conserve atoms with suitable coefficients; coefficients are omitted as requested. Molecular formulas represent neutral parent species, while actual protonation depends on pH. Sulfide photoreduction is represented with an elemental-sulfur redox endpoint, not an asserted measured sulfur-product distribution. Proposed screening conditions are distinguished from reported conditions and must not be interpreted as established productive operating windows. Cyanoacetylene supply, acrolein throughput, sequential reagent delivery, selective hydrolysis, and net glutamine accumulation remain unresolved. The glutamine-positive irradiation mixtures reported by Bizzarri et al. (2026) are important direct-detection evidence, but are not encoded as stoichiometric reactions because carbon incorporation and coproduct inventories are unresolved; no invented coproducts are added to force a balance. The provisional nitrate/pyruvate result of Chimiak et al. (2023) is likewise excluded from the conserved reaction layer, and the 2024 mineral-glycine study does not independently validate glutamine formation. The chemically undefined complex-glycine precursor of Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024), and unsupported selective glutamate activation, are not introduced as established intermediates or reactions. No oxygen-dependent reaction, enzyme, stereoselection, or validated environmental yield is assumed. The restricted role vocabulary requires coproducts and degradation sinks to be labeled intermediate.

reactions.name: Cyanoacetylene hydrocyanation: maleonitrile branch

conditions.temperature: 300 K model condition; exact experimental temperature is not specified in the supplied synopsis
conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous cyanide/ammonia chemistry. Proposed initial pH screen: 8-9.5. Cyanoacetylene must be supplied separately and captured before competing addition or polymerization; its concentration and delivery flux are unresolved boundary conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Net HCN addition across the activated carbon-carbon triple bond forms an unsaturated dinitrile. The graph follows the maleonitrile branch without asserting exclusive Z selectivity.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015), as summarized in the supplied research, support access to maleonitrile-containing C4 dinitrile products from cyanoacetylene and cyanide/ammonia chemistry. This node is a net product-channel representation, not a claim of a single elementary step or an isolated-product yield. Cyanoacetylene formation is outside the boundary: an oxygen-dependent oxidative coupling is not silently assumed.

reactions.name: Sulfide-driven photoreduction of maleonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-exposed pool; proposed pH screen 7-9. Sulfide is a consumed electron donor, not merely a catalyst. The supplied synopsis does not specify catalyst loading, wavelength, photon dose, or residence time. Copper availability must be checked against sulfide precipitation and cyanide complexation.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical electron and proton transfer reduces the alkene to succinonitrile. Oxidation of sulfide supplies reducing equivalents; elemental sulfur is the selected net redox endpoint.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 90% reduction of the unsaturated dinitrile under their experimental conditions. That reported yield is not assigned to the proposed environmental window. S8 requires proportional scaling of the inferred coefficients and introduces no conservation violation. Actual sulfur and copper speciation, UV attenuation, and competing photochemistry require measurement.

reactions.name: Partial photoreduction and hydrolysis of succinonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic staged UV irradiation; proposed pH screen 7-9. Irradiation must be terminated or the product transferred when aldehyde production peaks. No defensible environmental stopping time follows from the supplied synopsis. Subsequent cyanide capture should occur before aldehyde loss.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of one nitrile gives an imine-level intermediate; hydrolysis releases ammonia and forms 3-cyanopropanal while retaining the other nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support selective access to the semialdehyde, reported at approximately 89% under the study conditions. Ammonia and oxidized sulfur are included to make the modeled net reaction conserved. The sulfur endpoint is an idealized redox representation, not a measured sulfur mass balance. Overreduction, aldehyde reactions, and compatibility with residual copper/sulfide remain integration constraints.

reactions.name: Aldol condensation and dehydration to acrolein
agents: Hydroxide ions for general base catalysis

conditions.other: Anoxic neutral-to-basic water; proposed pH screen 8-10. Continuous formation followed by immediate cyanide trapping is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated concentration mechanism. Evaporation alone cannot be assumed to concentrate this reactive aldehyde without loss.

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde undergoes crossed aldol addition to formaldehyde, followed by dehydration of the beta-hydroxy aldehyde to acrolein.
reactions.reasoning: Cleaves (2003) supports low but measurable steady-state acrolein formation from dilute formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. This does not demonstrate production of the approximately 140 mM acrolein used in the concentrated downstream experiment of Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017). Aldehyde supply, competing aldol chemistry, acrolein polymerization, and capture efficiency prevent assigning an integrated pathway yield.

reactions.name: Cyanide conjugate addition to acrolein

conditions.temperature: 300 K model condition, close to the reported room-temperature experiment
conditions.other: Reported coupled addition/capture experiment: approximately 140 mM acrolein, 700 mM KCN, pH 9.2. The cyanide inventory serves both this step and rxn_006. These are laboratory concentrations, not demonstrated environmental concentrations.

reactions.mechanism: Conjugate cyanide addition and protonation convert acrolein into 3-cyanopropanal, which can be trapped immediately as its cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) support the acrolein/cyanide route. Their approximately 95% cyanohydrin result supports the coupled rxn_005-rxn_006 sequence, not a 95% isolated yield or environmental accumulation of 3-cyanopropanal. The aldehyde node represents a mechanistically justified transient intermediate.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin capture of 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: Cyanide-containing anoxic water. For the acrolein branch, pH 9.2 and the reported concentrated cyanide inventory apply to the coupled capture experiment. For the photochemical branch, separate reagent delivery is required; no equal concentration or yield is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl and the alkoxide is protonated, creating the fifth carbon of the future amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report efficient cyanohydrin formation from the semialdehyde; Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) support the same structural intermediate through acrolein chemistry. The reaction is reversible. A high capture yield does not establish long-term precursor storage or selective subsequent nitrile hydrolysis.

reactions.name: Strecker conversion to the five-carbon aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich anoxic solution; proposed pH screen 8-9.5. Cyanohydrin, aldehyde, imine, HCN, and cyanide equilibrate. Free-ammonia availability, volatile losses, and the required reaction time must be measured. This stage need not remain UV-exposed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin dissociation permits aldehyde-imine equilibration; cyanide addition to the imine gives the alpha-aminonitrile. The net reaction is not direct displacement of hydroxide from a stable cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) support access to the common glutamine/glutamate aminodinitrile precursor. The approximately 70% figure summarized for the last two Patel transformations is not a free-glutamine yield. This is the strongest supported advanced endpoint in the conserved synthesis graph.

reactions.name: Candidate alpha-nitrile hydration

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K proposed screening range; no productive window established
conditions.other: Separate dark, anoxic acidic stage; proposed pH screen 2-4. Measure both nitrile positions, amide products, residual precursor, and decomposition over a time course. Do not assume that the alpha-amino group supplies adequate regioselectivity.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the nitrile adjacent to the amino-bearing carbon gives an alpha-carboxamide while the terminal nitrile remains intact.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE for this substrate and selectivity. Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) establish the precursor, not this selective conversion. General alpha-aminonitrile hydration chemistry motivates testing this branch, but does not establish preferential reaction, useful rate, or an isolable product distribution.

reactions.name: Candidate alpha-carboxamide hydrolysis with terminal-nitrile retention
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed amide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Dark anoxic acidic water; proposed pH screen 1-3. The terminal nitrile must survive conditions sufficient to hydrolyze the alpha amide. Cool and change conditions before attempting rxn_010. Neither the required residence time nor useful selectivity is established.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to the protonated alpha amide, followed by carbon-nitrogen cleavage, forms the alpha carboxylic acid and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE substrate-specific kinetic discrimination. Amide hydrolysis is chemically standard, but no study in the supplied research establishes retention of this terminal nitrile during the required conversion. The precursor papers, Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017), do not validate this step. Its possible advantage is postponing formation of the glutamine side-chain amide until after alpha-carboxyl formation.

reactions.name: Candidate terminal-nitrile hydration to glutamine

conditions.temperature: 300-320 K proposed screen; no demonstrated glutamine-producing window
conditions.other: Dark anoxic aqueous stage; proposed pH screen 2-5. Quantify nitrile disappearance, glutamine appearance, glutamate, and pyroglutamate simultaneously. Any recovered glutamine should be assessed after transfer to approximately 300 K, near-neutral shaded water; that transfer is not an established preservation protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Partial hydration converts the remaining nitrile to the side-chain primary amide without further hydrolysis to a carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE and target-limiting. Neither Patel et al. (2015) nor Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) establishes this substrate-specific productive stopping point. Formation of an amide as a transient hydrolysis intermediate is plausible, but recoverable glutamine requires its formation rate to exceed subsequent hydrolysis and cyclization. No yield or accumulation claim is justified.

reactions.name: Candidate terminal-first hydration of the aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Dark anoxic water; proposed pH screen 2-4. Analyze both regioisomeric monoamides rather than identifying them from molecular mass alone. No selective catalyst for terminal-first hydration is established.

reactions.mechanism: Water converts the terminal nitrile into the future glutamine side-chain amide while leaving the alpha nitrile unchanged.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE, and not assumed to be the favored hydration branch. The supplied precursor studies, Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017), do not demonstrate this regioselectivity. This edge represents a chemically possible product channel to test, not an independently validated synthesis.

reactions.name: Candidate alpha-nitrile hydration of glutamine alpha-nitrile

conditions.other: Dark anoxic water; proposed pH screen 2-4. Track alpha-nitrile hydration separately from side-chain amide hydrolysis. No rate ratio or permissible residence time is available from the supplied research.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the remaining alpha nitrile produces 2-aminopentanediamide.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE substrate-specific extension of aminonitrile hydration. Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) motivate the nitrile framework but do not validate preservation of a pre-existing side-chain amide during this conversion. The diamide is not glutamine and still requires differential amide hydrolysis.

reactions.name: Candidate terminal-nitrile hydration of the alpha-carboxamide

conditions.other: Dark anoxic acidic water; proposed pH screen 2-4. Competing alpha-amide hydrolysis would divert material toward mol_016; continued side-chain hydrolysis would also change the product inventory.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the residual terminal nitrile produces the same diamide reached by rxn_012, but through the opposite order of nitrile hydration.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE kinetic branch. No supplied study demonstrates useful accumulation of this diamide through this ordering. Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) support only the upstream precursor chemistry. The alternative ordering is structurally distinct but is not additional experimental validation.

reactions.name: Candidate selective alpha-amide hydrolysis of the diamide
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed amide hydrolysis

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K exploratory screen; no selective operating window established
conditions.other: Dark anoxic water; proposed pH screen 1-4. Determine hydrolysis at both amides, formation of either monoacid regioisomer, glutamate production, and cyclization. Heating to accelerate conversion cannot be assumed compatible with glutamine survival.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the alpha carboxamide creates the amino-acid carboxyl group while the terminal carboxamide remains intact.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE and a decisive unresolved bottleneck. Atom balance does not establish discrimination between the two primary amides. The supplied research explicitly identifies differential hydrolysis as unresolved; Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) do not demonstrate this free-glutamine-forming step. No mineral, activating reagent, or numerical yield is assigned without evidence.

reactions.name: Candidate side-chain nitrile hydration at the cyanohydrin stage

conditions.other: Dark anoxic acidic water; proposed pH screen 2-4. Measure cyanohydrin dissociation, hydration of either nitrile, and aldehyde-derived side products. No preferential terminal hydration is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the nitrile remote from the hydroxyl-bearing carbon forms the side-chain amide before the amino group is introduced.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE early-amide alternative, not reported as a demonstrated glutamine route in the supplied literature. Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) support mol_013, but not this transformation. Its chemical purpose is to test whether moving side-chain amide formation ahead of Strecker conversion changes the selectivity problem; it does not eliminate that problem.

reactions.name: Candidate Strecker conversion of the amide-bearing cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Anoxic ammonia-containing water; proposed pH screen 8-9.5 following a separate hydration stage. Cyanohydrin dissociation, imine formation, and cyanide recapture must outcompete aldehyde oligomerization and amide loss.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin opening allows imine formation with ammonia; cyanide addition gives the amide-bearing alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE for this particular amide-bearing substrate. The mechanism is an analogy to the experimentally supported nitrile-bearing Strecker sequence in Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017), not a result those papers establish for mol_019. Preserving an existing amide is chemically plausible at mild conditions, but conversion, competing chemistry, and environmental flux are unmeasured.

reactions.name: Candidate nitrile hydration before cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Separate dark anoxic aqueous stage; proposed pH screen 2-4. Determine whether nitrile hydration occurs before aldehyde loss and whether further amide hydrolysis can be avoided. No isolated-aldehyde accumulation is presumed.

reactions.mechanism: Partial hydration of the only nitrile in 3-cyanopropanal produces 4-oxobutanamide while retaining aldehyde reactivity.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE alternative with a specific chemical motivation: only one nitrile is present, so regioselectivity between two nitriles is avoided at this stage. It instead requires aldehyde survival and control of hydration extent. Patel et al. (2015) and Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) support access to the starting aldehyde or its trapped form, not this amide-aldehyde conversion or its isolation.

reactions.name: Candidate cyanohydrin formation from 4-oxobutanamide

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanide-containing water; proposed pH screen 8-9.5. Establish the equilibrium and capture rate for this substrate directly rather than transferring the reported 95% acrolein-system yield.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition to the aldehyde carbonyl and protonation create the amide-bearing cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE substrate-specific application of ordinary cyanohydrin chemistry. Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) and Patel et al. (2015) support the analogous aldehyde capture with a terminal nitrile, not this terminal-amide substrate. A remote amide does not obviously preclude carbonyl addition, but the supplied research provides no measured equilibrium, yield, or integrated glutamine synthesis for this step.

reactions.name: Competing glutamine side-chain hydrolysis

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K loss-characterization range, not a recommended storage range
conditions.other: Occurs to a condition-dependent extent; acid, base, and heating can accelerate loss. Quantify alongside synthesis. Approximately 300 K and near-neutral shaded water are preservation hypotheses, not proof that production exceeds destruction.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the side-chain carboxamide releases ammonia and forms glutamic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Kuroda and Kobayashi (2024) discuss hydrolysis progressing from glutamine toward glutamate in their proposed framework, and the supplied research identifies glutamine hydrolysis as a central loss process. The chemistry is well founded, but rates and product fractions for this network remain unspecified and must be measured. Including this edge does not demonstrate accumulation.

reactions.name: Competing glutamine cyclization to pyroglutamate

conditions.other: Dark or illuminated anoxic water; evaluate pH and temperature dependence independently. Warmer or concentrated stages may increase loss. No quantitative rate or safe residence time is inferred from the supplied synopsis.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack of the alpha amino group on the side-chain amide carbonyl forms a five-membered lactam and releases ammonia; the net reaction is not dehydration.
reactions.reasoning: This is a chemically justified competing-loss mechanism described in the supplied research. Its kinetic implementation here is SPECULATIVE: the supplied hydrothermal-decomposition discussion does not identify an author-year primary reference that can be assigned reliably to this specific reaction, and no citation is invented. Measuring pyroglutamate is necessary to distinguish target formation from subsequent disappearance.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic entry with alpha-carboxyl formation before side-chain amidation
pathways.description: Conditional route. Literature-supported precursor construction is followed by alpha-nitrile hydration, alpha-amide hydrolysis, and final terminal-nitrile hydration. It avoids exposing an already formed glutamine side-chain amide to the alpha-amide hydrolysis stage, but rxn_008-rxn_010 are unvalidated as a compatible selective sequence. No end-to-end yield or accumulation is established.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry with alpha-carboxyl formation before side-chain amidation
pathways.description: Conditional route sharing the terminal sequence of P1 but constructing the carbon skeleton through aldehyde condensation and acrolein hydrocyanation. Low steady-state acrolein production has not been operationally connected to the concentrated cyanide capture experiment. The final three transformations remain unvalidated.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic entry with terminal-first aminodinitrile hydration
pathways.description: Conditional route that forms the side-chain amide on the aminodinitrile, then hydrates the alpha nitrile and hydrolyzes the resulting alpha amide. Both terminal-first hydration and selective diamide hydrolysis are unresolved. This ordering is not an independently demonstrated synthesis.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry with terminal-first aminodinitrile hydration
pathways.description: Conditional acrolein-based counterpart of P3. The measured coupled cyanide capture supports precursor accessibility only; it does not establish the terminal-first hydration branch or preservation of the side-chain amide during conversion of the alpha functionality.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic entry with alpha-first diamide formation
pathways.description: Conditional route that hydrates the alpha nitrile first and the terminal nitrile second, then attempts selective alpha-amide hydrolysis. It differs from P3 in the order of the first two hydrations, but shares the same unvalidated diamide-to-glutamine bottleneck.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry with alpha-first diamide formation
pathways.description: Conditional acrolein-based counterpart of P5. This route inherits the upstream concentration mismatch and requires productive diamide formation followed by selective alpha-amide hydrolysis. Neither an integrated operating window nor free-glutamine accumulation is established.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic entry with side-chain amidation at the cyanohydrin stage
pathways.description: Conditional early-amide route. The terminal nitrile is hydrated before Strecker conversion, generating an amide-bearing cyanohydrin. Its formation and subsequent Strecker reaction are substrate-specific hypotheses, and final selective diamide hydrolysis remains necessary.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry with side-chain amidation at the cyanohydrin stage
pathways.description: Conditional acrolein-based counterpart of P7. Experimentally supported access to the nitrile-bearing cyanohydrin does not validate its selective terminal hydration. This route tests a different timing of amide installation rather than supplying independent evidence for glutamine synthesis.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic entry with side-chain amidation before carbonyl capture
pathways.description: Conditional route that hydrates the sole nitrile of 3-cyanopropanal before adding the fifth carbon through cyanohydrin formation. This avoids two-nitrile regioselectivity during initial amide installation, but requires aldehyde survival, partial rather than exhaustive hydrolysis, and later selective alpha-amide hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Acrolein entry with side-chain amidation before carbonyl capture
pathways.description: Conditional acrolein-based counterpart of P9. Unlike the reported rapid cyanohydrin trapping experiment, this route requires the transient Michael-addition aldehyde to undergo nitrile hydration first. That operational diversion is untested and may be kinetically unfavorable. The terminal glutamine-forming hydrolysis is also unvalidated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a connected, atom-balanced route with experimentally supported precursor chemistry through mol_014, according to the supplied account of Patel et al. (2015). The decisive difficulty is rxn_009: converting the alpha-carboxamide to a carboxyl group while retaining the terminal nitrile requires an unestablished kinetic window. rxn_010 must subsequently hydrate that nitrile without substantial progression beyond glutamine. Neither transformation is established by demonstrating aminodinitrile formation. Surface placement is compatible with the precursor photochemistry, but the submitted entries do not specify conditions that reconcile hydrolysis with product preservation.
suggestions: Measure competing nitrile hydration, amide hydrolysis and cyclization rates for mol_014, mol_015 and mol_016 at explicitly stated pH, temperature and residence time.
Attach reaction-specific experimental references and specify UV exposure, sulfide concentration, copper speciation if used, and a physically justified reagent-delivery schedule.
Demonstrate free-glutamine formation and persistence while quantifying glutamate and pyroglutamate alongside the intended intermediates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon-skeleton assembly is chemically coherent. Cleaves (2003) supports acrolein production from the stated aldehydes, but at low steady-state abundance; the concentrated cyanide-capture conditions summarized for Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) do not establish integrated throughput from that source. The reported high cyanohydrin yield supports the coupled rxn_005/rxn_006 chemistry, not the complete glutamine pathway. As in P1, rxn_009 and rxn_010 impose unresolved differential-hydrolysis requirements. All reactions conserve atoms and charge under the supplied check.
suggestions: Demonstrate cyanide capture using acrolein generated by rxn_004, with measured losses to polymerization and competing aldehyde chemistry.
Justify the concentrations and pH used for capture rather than transferring the reported approximately 700 mM cyanide result directly to unspecified surface water.
Establish sequential operating windows for alpha-carboxamide hydrolysis and terminal-nitrile hydration, including glutamine production-versus-degradation kinetics.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The terminal-first sequence is atom-balanced and identifies chemically meaningful intermediates, but the supplied literature does not establish its substrate-specific hydration rates or product distribution. Terminal-first hydration need not be exclusive for the complete network to function, because the alpha-first branch can also reach mol_017. The principal unresolved requirement is therefore rxn_014: selective alpha-amide hydrolysis of the diamide while preserving the side-chain amide. Patel et al. (2015) supports the upstream aminodinitrile chemistry, not this complete hydrolysis sequence.
suggestions: Measure both initial hydration branches and distinguish mol_015 from mol_018 analytically; exclusive terminal-first selectivity is not required if both branches remain productive.
Test mol_017 directly for selective glutamine formation, including competing side-chain hydrolysis and cyclization.
Specify conditions and staging that separate productive photochemistry from hydrolysis and glutamine preservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acrolein entry has experimental precedent, but its integration with low-throughput aldehyde condensation and the required cyanide concentrations remains unestablished. The terminal-first hydration branch is a plausible hypothesis rather than a demonstrated continuation of Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017). Mixed initial hydration products would not necessarily invalidate the network, but formation of a diamide does not establish selective conversion to glutamine in rxn_014. The surface designation alone does not demonstrate compatible conditions for these stages.
suggestions: Quantify capture of continuously generated or episodically supplied acrolein at justified concentrations, including competing reactions.
Measure hydration branching and subsequent diamide formation rather than assuming the terminal-first ordering.
Identify and experimentally validate a realistic condition or catalyst system for rxn_014, with glutamine selectivity and survival measured together.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is marginally the strongest experimental starting hypothesis among the submitted pathways, not a validated synthesis. Alpha-aminonitrile hydration is motivated by the supplied literature, and proceeding through the diamide avoids requiring alpha-amide hydrolysis while a terminal nitrile remains intact, as in rxn_009. Initial hydration mixtures could also contribute to diamide formation. Nevertheless, rxn_014 remains a decisive unsupported step: no demonstrated operating window or catalyst selectively converts the alpha-carboxamide to the acid while preserving the side-chain amide. The ranking is provisional pending comparative kinetic measurements.
suggestions: Prioritize direct experiments on mol_017, measuring glutamine, glutamate, partially hydrolyzed isomers and cyclic products over time.
Determine whether controlled nitrile hydration produces the diamide faster than competing amide hydrolysis under realistic aqueous conditions.
Document reaction-specific literature support, photochemical conditions, catalyst availability and the physical implementation of any staged processing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines the experimentally grounded acrolein/cyanide entry with the comparatively coherent diamide hypothesis. Its limitations are integrated acrolein throughput, the absence of demonstrated hydration conditions, and especially selective diamide hydrolysis in rxn_014. The high-yield precursor capture described by Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) cannot be assigned to the downstream glutamine-forming sequence. The pathway is structurally and stoichiometrically valid, but neither free-glutamine production nor a favorable production-to-loss balance is established.
suggestions: Connect measured acrolein-generation flux to cyanide-capture performance without assuming laboratory concentrations arise automatically.
Validate diamide formation and selective alpha-amide hydrolysis using authentic standards and time-resolved product analysis.
Test the assembled sequence under specified, physically achievable conditions and include the competing glutamine degradation reactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The graph route is valid, but hydration at the cyanohydrin stage adds an untested substrate-compatibility problem. rxn_015 must produce the intended side-chain amide while accounting for the other nitrile, cyanohydrin reversibility and competing hydrolysis. rxn_016 is plausible as a net Strecker transformation through carbonyl/imine equilibria, not as an established direct replacement of hydroxyl by ammonia. Neither proposed step is validated by the supplied precursor studies. The pathway also retains the unresolved final selectivity requirement in rxn_014.
suggestions: Characterize the products of mol_013 hydration and distinguish mol_019 from alternative nitrile-hydration products.
Demonstrate conversion of the amide-bearing cyanohydrin to mol_018, measuring cyanohydrin reversal, carbonyl availability and side reactions.
Validate the subsequent diamide-to-glutamine step rather than treating earlier side-chain amidation as resolving final selectivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supported acrolein-to-cyanohydrin chemistry does not establish that the cyanohydrin tolerates selective side-chain nitrile hydration or subsequent amide-bearing Strecker chemistry. These are explicitly acknowledged but consequential departures from the demonstrated sequence. Low acrolein throughput and the concentrated capture conditions remain additional integration uncertainties. Even successful rxn_015 and rxn_016 would only deliver a precursor to the still-unvalidated selective hydrolysis in rxn_014.
suggestions: Test cyanohydrin hydration in chemically realistic acrolein-capture mixtures, including residual cyanide and aldehyde-derived side products.
Establish mol_019 and mol_018 identities and yields before assigning productive flux to this branch.
Specify compatible hydration, Strecker and final hydrolysis conditions, with direct measurement of glutamine accumulation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrating mol_012 before cyanohydrin formation avoids choosing between two nitriles at that stage, which is a genuine chemical distinction. It instead requires productive nitrile hydration while preserving a reactive aldehyde, and the supplied research does not demonstrate rxn_017. Cyanohydrin formation in rxn_018 is chemically plausible, but the availability and lifetime of open-chain mol_020 should be established, including possible hydration or intramolecular cyclization. The later Strecker conversion and selective diamide hydrolysis remain unvalidated.
suggestions: Measure whether mol_012 can form mol_020 faster than competing aldehyde reactions under an explicitly justified hydration regime.
Characterize mol_020 speciation and demonstrate productive cyanohydrin capture rather than assuming the nominal aldehyde structure determines its availability.
Validate conversion through mol_018 and mol_017 to free glutamine, including final-step selectivity and degradation kinetics.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The atom-balanced early-amidation strategy is conceptually coherent, but the cited acrolein experiment primarily supports rapid cyanide capture toward the cyanohydrin, not diversion of the aldehyde intermediate into rxn_017. This route requires an unestablished processing window in which nitrile hydration competes successfully with carbonyl capture and other aldehyde reactions. Acrolein supply-to-capture throughput, amide-bearing Strecker chemistry and selective final diamide hydrolysis all remain unresolved. The shorter listed sequence does not independently improve its evidentiary support.
suggestions: Establish conditions that make mol_012 available for hydration before cyanohydrin capture, including a physically justified reagent-delivery or separation mechanism if needed.
Demonstrate mol_020 formation and subsequent cyanohydrin/Strecker conversion with full product accounting.
Measure selective glutamine production from the diamide and compare its rate with hydrolysis and cyclization losses.

evaluation.network_feedback: NOT APPROVED under the required network confidence threshold of 0.9. Structural validity is excellent: the 23 molecule nodes and 20 reaction nodes form a connected network, molecule IDs are consistent, and the corrected five-carbon aminodinitrile is appropriate for glutamine. The deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction. The coefficients of 8 in rxn_002 and rxn_003 arise naturally from the S8 representation and are not conservation defects; the sulfur-product distribution remains an acknowledged mechanistic idealization. Literature alignment is strong in distinguishing demonstrated precursor synthesis, direct glutamine detection in different systems, and unvalidated proposals. However, the submitted reaction entries lack reaction-specific citations and quantitative operating conditions. The surface designation permits UV chemistry but does not establish compatible pH, temperature, concentrations, catalyst speciation, irradiation or residence times. No interenvironment transfer is claimed, so none is penalized. At the complete-network level, mixed initial nitrile hydration need not be fatal because both branches can reach the diamide; exclusive early regioselectivity is therefore not required. The unresolved bottleneck is productive formation of the alpha-carboxyl group while retaining the side-chain amide, through rxn_009/rxn_010 or rxn_014. The credible degradation reactions rxn_019 and rxn_020 further require a measured production-versus-loss balance, without implying that glutamine necessarily decomposes rapidly under every surface condition. The supplied Bizzarri et al. detection evidence does not validate these encoded transformations. Ten conditional routes neither multiply the experimental evidence nor resolve their common chemical limitations. P5 is only a marginally preferred testing hypothesis. Approval requires at least one experimentally supported, environmentally specified complete route to identified free glutamine with demonstrated persistence or accumulation.
